That is: the samuṭṭhāna and the rest are the same as in the padasodhamma rule. The difference is that here it is kiriyākiriya.

Vesālī · Mahāvana (the Great Wood)

The monks who were friends and spent the rains on the bank of the Vaggumudā river, in order to get food during the famine in the Vajji country, praised each other's superhuman states to lay people.

When the rains were over and they came to Vesālī, the other monks were thin and pale, but these monks were bright and healthy. The Buddha questioned them and asked, “Is it true?” When they said, “Yes, venerable sir,” he rebuked them and laid down final rule:

The training rule“Yo pana bhikkhu anupasampannassa uttarimanussadhammaṃ āroceyya, bhūtasmiṃ pācittiyaṃ.”
That is: the Dhamma of meditators and of noble ones, of the kind stated in the fourth pārājika.
That is: apart from Bhikkhu and Bhikkhuni, all others are unordained.
That is: when one really has states such as jhāna, telling it to someone other than monks and nuns brings a pācittiya.

secs.t: (D) The laying down of the rule and the division of offences
secs.h:
That is: it was laid down not at Sāvatthī but at Vesālī, concerning the monks who lived on the bank of the Vaggumudā. It is a common rule; it is anāṇattika.

SituationOffence
Telling an unordained person directly (nippariyāya) about a real jhāna and so on, when he understands it at oncePācittiya
When he does not understand itDukkaṭa
Telling it indirectly (pariyāya — by a hint, in a roundabout way) — whether he understands or notDukkaṭa

Anāpatti That is: there is no offence in telling an ordained person when there is such a reason, nor for the first offender. Telling lay people about another monk's superhuman state is a dukkaṭa.
Why the insane are not included here Because noble ones are never insane, and because those who have attained jhāna would then fall away from their jhāna — for these reasons they are not included here.

1
The superhuman state is real (true).
2
Announcing it to an unordained person.
3
Taṅkhaṇa vijānana — understanding it at that very moment.
4
Anaññāpadesa — saying it directly, not in some other way.

It arises from bhūtārocana; it is kiriyā; nosaññāvimokkha; acittaka; paṇṇattivajja; kāyakamma and vacīkamma; it has two kinds of mind (dvicitta) — wholesome and indeterminate (kusala, abyākata); and two kinds of feeling (dvivedana) — pleasant and neutral (sukha, majjhatta).

Sāvatthī · Jetavana monastery

Ven. Upananda Sakyaputta quarrelled with the group-of-six monks. After that, he committed a sañcetanika sukkavissaṭṭhi offence, and for that offence he asked the Saṅgha for parivāsa and received it.

At that time a guild in Sāvatthī gave a meal to the Saṅgha. Ven. Upananda, who was observing parivāsa, sat on the last seat in the dining hall.

Then the group-of-six monks said to the lay followers: “This Ven. Upananda Sakyaputta is your respected family monk. With the very hand with which he eats food given in faith, he released impurity. He committed a sañcetanika sukkavissaṭṭhi offence and asked the Saṅgha for parivāsa; that is why he sits on the last seat, observing parivāsa.”

The monks of few wishes criticised this and told the Blessed One. He questioned them and rebuked them, saying: “Foolish men, how could you tell a monk's duṭṭhulla offence to an unordained person?”

The training rule“Yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhussa duṭṭhullaṃ āpattiṃ anupasampannassa āroceyya, aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā, pācittiyaṃ.”
That is: the offence of a monk who has not fallen into pārājika (who is not pārājika).
That is: in general, the word duṭṭhulla is used for two groups of offences (pārājika and saṅghādisesa), but in this rule only saṅghādisesa is meant.

Anupasampanna = all others except ordained Bhikkhu and Bhikkhuni.

Āroceyya = telling 

Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā = except with the monks' agreement (sammuti).

That is: for a monk who commits offences again and again, for his restraint in the future — making a limit of offences and of families, or not making one — having announced it (apalokana) three times, [the monks make] a katikā (an agreement).

Decision of offences:

SituationOffence
When it is limited by offences, telling other offencesPācittiya
When it is limited by families, telling it to other familiesPācittiya
When it is limited by both, telling it beyond one of themPācittiya
When it is limited by neitherNo offence

secs.t: (E) The laying down of the rule and the division of offences
secs.h:
That is: it was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six monks. It is a common rule; it is anāṇattika; it is a tika-pācittiya.

SituationOffence
A saṅghādisesa offence — with the perception “duṭṭhulla” / in doubt / with the perception “aduṭṭhulla” — told to an unordained person, without the agreementPācittiya (tika)​
An offence that is not duṭṭhulla — with the perception “duṭṭhulla”, or in doubtDukkaṭa
Telling the other six groups of offencesDukkaṭa
Telling the duṭṭhulla or aduṭṭhulla misconduct (ajjhācāra) of an unordained personDukkaṭa
Telling a minor offenceDukkaṭa

Anāpatti

CaseResult
Vatthumattaṃ — telling only the basis (the act) of the offence, without telling the group of offence.No offence
Āpattimattaṃ — telling only the group of offence, without telling the basis.No offence
When there is a bhikkhu sammuti — telling without going beyond the limit of the agreement.No offence
For the insane and so on.No offence
For the first offenders.No offence

1
The saṅghādisesa offence, with its basis (savatthuka), of a monk of the stated kind.
2
Announcing it to an unordained person.
3
No bhikkhu sammuti.

Āḷavī · Aggāḷava shrine

The monks of Āḷavī, doing new building work, dug the earth and had it dug.

People criticised them, saying: “The Sakyan recluses dig the earth and have it dug; they harm beings with one faculty.”

The monks of few wishes criticised this and told the Blessed One. He questioned them, rebuked them, and said:

The training rule“Yo pana bhikkhu paṭhaviṃ khaṇeyya vā khaṇāpeyya vā, pācittiyaṃ.”

secs.t: (A) Jāta paṭhavī is of three kinds — pure, mixed, heaped
secs.h:
Suddhapaṭhavī = soil or clay that is pure by nature.

Missapaṭhavī = soil in which, within the soil or clay, one third is stones, gravel, potsherds, laterite or sand.

Puñjapaṭhavī = a heap of soil or clay wetted by rain for more than four months.

That is: if these three kinds are not burnt, they are “jāta paṭhavī”; if burnt, or if stones and so on are mixed in more than the set amount, it is ajāta paṭhavī.

Jāta paṭhavī is soil that is not allowable to dig.
That is: if he digs himself, or destroys it by khaṇana (digging), bhedana (breaking), vilekhana (scratching), pacana (burning) and so on — there is a pācittiya for each effort.
That is: for one who orders, “Dig this place”, “Dig this soil” and so on, there is a pācittiya.

SituationOffence
Earth — perception “earth” — digs / has it dug, breaks / has it broken, burns / has it burntPācittiya
Earth — in doubtDukkaṭa
Earth — perception “not earth”No offence
Not earth — perception “earth”Dukkaṭa
Not earth — in doubtDukkaṭa
Not earth — perception “not earth”No offence

Anāpatti

CaseResult
Saying things like “Please know this” / “There is a use for this” / “Please make this allowable” (allowable words).No offence
Asañcicca — without intending it (for example, if soil breaks when a tree is dragged with a stick).No offence
Asatiyā — without mindfulness (scratching by turning the foot, and so on).No offence
Ajānantassa — not knowing that it is jāta paṭhavī.No offence
Not fixing the place — saying things like “Dig a pond, dig a pit, dig a yam”.No offence
Destroying ajāta paṭhavī — burnt clay, gokaṇṭaka, soil that has broken and fallen from a river bank, lumps of clay cut by a plough, and so on.No offence
For the insane and so on; for the first offenders.No offence

1
It is jāta paṭhavī.
2
The perception of earth.
3
Digging it oneself, or having it dug.

The samuṭṭhāna and the rest are the same as in the Adinnādāna rule (the second pārājika).

This is paṇṇattivajja; ticitta (three kinds of mind); tivedana (three kinds of feeling).

Āḷavī · Aggāḷava shrine

The Āḷavaka monks, doing new building work, cut trees and had them cut. While one monk was cutting a tree, the female deity living in it said: “Venerable sir, wishing to build a dwelling for yourself, do not cut my dwelling.” He paid no attention and cut it down; then the blow struck the arm of the deity's child.

She thought of killing the monk, but she thought, “That is not proper for me; I will tell this to the Blessed One,” and went and told him. People criticised: “The Sakyan recluses cut trees, which are life with one faculty, and have them cut.” When the monks of few wishes reported this, the Blessed One rebuked [them] and laid down the training rule:

The training rule“Bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ.”

The five kinds of seeds (bhūtagāma) shown in the Pāli:

Kind of seedExamples
MūlabījaTurmeric, ginger, vacā, ativisa, usīra and so on — things that grow from the root
KhandhabījaAssattha, nigrodha, pilakkha, udumbara, kapittha and so on — things that grow from the trunk
PhaḷubījaSugarcane, bamboo, reed (naḷa) and so on — things that grow from the joints
AggabījaAjjuka, phaṇijjaka, hirivera and so on — things that grow from the tip
BījabījaPubbaṇṇa, aparaṇṇa (grains) and so on — things that grow from the seed itself

Things that have arisen, are growing, are born and have grown are called bhūta. “Gāma” has the meaning of “a heap”; it is a name for green grass, trees and so on that are rooted in place.

“Pātabyatā” means being able to use something as one likes, by cutting, breaking and so on.

A monk who destroys a bhūtagāma that is not dried up — growing on the ground, in water, on walls and so on — even a tiny grass, a mustard seed, or moss, by pulling it out, cutting it, piercing it and so on, or who has it done in the way said in the earth-digging rule, falls into a pācittiya.

secs.t: (C) The laying down of the rule and the command
secs.h:
It was laid down at Āḷavī concerning the Āḷavaka monks, on the matter of cutting trees.

It is a common rule; it is sāṇattika (the offence also arises by getting another person to do it).

secs.t: (D) Division of offences — according to the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
secs.h:
CaseOffence
Knowing a bhūtagāma to be a bhūtagāma, destroying it by cutting / breaking / cooking and so on, or having it donePācittiya
Destroying roots, trunks, joints, tips or seeds that are separated from the bhūtagāma (in a container, in a heap, or planted in the ground) — when only the root / shoot has come out, when a leaf stalk the size of a span (vidatthi) has come out, or when the shoot is not yet greenDukkaṭa
Destroying it while in doubt about bhūtagāma / bījagāmaDukkaṭa
Destroying something that is not bhūtagāma / bījagāma, thinking that it is, or in doubtDukkaṭa
Destroying it while thinking otherwise in both cases (with atathā saññā — a wrong perception)No offence

Anāpatti

CaseResult
Saying “Cut a tree, cut a creeper” and so on, without fixing “this tree”.No offence
Saying “Know this, give this, bring this, there is a need for this, make it allowable”.No offence
Destroying it without intending to, without mindfulness, or without knowing.No offence
For the insane and so on.No offence

Seed-kinds that have been separated from the bhūtagāma with an allowable word should also be used only after having them made allowable again by saying “kappiyaṃ karohi”; then they are also free from bījagāma.

1
Making allowable should be done with fire, with a nail, or with a blade.
2
With fire — making it touch on one side and saying “kappiya”.
3
With a blade — even a needle; showing a piercing or a cut made with the point or the edge of a sharp blade.
4
With a nail — except the hooves of cattle, buffaloes and so on, with a human or animal nail that is not rotten, in the same way as said for the blade.
5
If a heap of seeds, a thousand trees, or a big load of sugarcane are tied together, when one is made allowable, all are made allowable; but piercing the creeper that ties the load is not valid.
6
In rice mixed with chillies and so on, or in sesame, rice and so on, piercing one is enough; those put into gruel should be pierced one by one.
7
In fruits such as the wood-apple (kapiṭṭha), if the inner pulp moves, it should be broken and then made allowable; if it is joined together, it can be done on the shell.
8
For a young fruit, a fruit with no seed, or a fruit to be eaten after taking out the seed, making allowable is not needed.

1
It is a bhūtagāma.
2
Having the perception of bhūtagāma.
3
Destroying it, or having it destroyed.
The same as in the earth-digging rule.

Kosambī · Ghositārāma

Ven. Channa behaved wrongly. When he was questioned about the offence in the midst of the Saṅgha, he said, “Who? What? How?” and covered one thing with another. The Blessed One rebuked him, allowed the aññavādaka act, and laid down the training rule:

“Aññavādake pācittiyaṃ.”

Later, because Ven. Channa troubled the Saṅgha by staying silent, the Blessed One had the vihesaka act imposed and added to the rule:

The final training rule“Aññavādake vihesake pācittiyaṃ.”
In the midst of the Saṅgha, saying something other than what the Vinaya expert asks is aññavādaka; troubling the Saṅgha by staying silent (tuṇhībhāva) is vihesaka.

When a monk who has fallen into an offence is questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha, if — not wishing to tell — he covers it with other words, or stays silent and troubles [the Saṅgha], then after the Saṅgha has done the aññavādaka / vihesaka act for that, when he does so again there is a pācittiya. (In the two matters there are two pācittiyas.)

secs.t: (C) The laying down of the rule and the command
secs.h:
It was laid down at Kosambī concerning Ven. Channa.

It is a common rule; it is anāṇattika.

In a legitimate act (dhammakamma) it is a tika-pācittiya; in an illegitimate act (adhammakamma) it is a tika-dukkaṭa.

secs.t: (D) Division of offences — according to the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
secs.h:
CaseOffence
After it has been imposed by a legitimate act (in all three: perceiving it as a legitimate act, in doubt, perceiving it as an illegitimate act), covering it with something else in the same way, or staying silentPācittiya
Doing so when it was imposed by an illegitimate actDukkaṭa
Doing so before it is imposedDukkaṭa

Anāpatti

CaseResult
For one who, not knowing about the offence, asks, “What are you saying?”No offence
For one who does not speak because he is sick.No offence
For one who does not speak with the thought, “There will be quarrels and so on in the Saṅgha.”No offence
For one who does not speak with the thought, “They are doing an act unlawfully, by a faction, or against one who is not suitable.”No offence
For the insane and so on.No offence

1
The act has been imposed by a legitimate act.
2
Being questioned about the offence or about the matter.
3
With the wish to hide it, covering it with something else, or staying silent.
As in the Adinnādāna rule. Sometimes it happens by doing, sometimes by not doing. The feeling is painful (dukkha).

pac13.title_en: Making Others Look Down on a Monk

secs.h:
Rājagaha · Veḷuvana

Ven. Dabba Mallaputta assigned lodgings and assigned meals. The Mettiya-Bhūmajaka monks, who received poor lodgings and poor meals, made the monks look down on him, saying, “He does it out of favouritism.” The Blessed One rebuked them and laid down:

“Ujjhāpanake pācittiyaṃ.”

Later, because they criticised him (khiyyana) while staying near the monks, he added to the rule:

The final training rule“Ujjhāpanake khiyyanake pācittiyaṃ.”

Wishing for the disgrace of an ordained monk who has been appointed by the Saṅgha — such as the one who assigns lodgings — and making other monks look down on him and think of him as low, is ujjhāpanaka.

Speaking dispraise of him everywhere is khiyyanaka.

For one who, wishing for the disgrace of the appointed monk, speaks to an ordained monk and makes him look down on that monk, or criticises that monk — there is a pācittiya. (In the two matters there are two pācittiyas.)

secs.t: (C) The laying down of the rule and the command
secs.h:
It was laid down at Rājagaha concerning the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka monks.

It is a common rule; it is anāṇattika.

secs.t: (D) Division of offences — according to the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
secs.h:
CaseOffence
Wishing for the dispraise of an ordained monk appointed by a legitimate act, making [others] look down on him / criticising him near an ordained monk (in all three perceptions)Pācittiya
Doing so when the act of appointment is an illegitimate actDukkaṭa
Saying so near an unordained personDukkaṭa
Speaking dispraise of an ordained monk who is not appointed, near anyoneDukkaṭa
Speaking dispraise of an unordained person (whether appointed or not), near anyoneDukkaṭa

Anāpatti There is no offence for one who makes others look down on, or criticises, a person who by nature acts with bias such as favouritism (chanda and the other agati); nor for the insane and so on.

1
Being appointed by a legitimate act.
2
Being ordained.
3
Not going on a wrong course (agatigamana).
4
Wishing for his dispraise.
5
The person near whom one speaks is ordained.
6
Ujjhāpana or khiyyana.
As in the Adinnādāna rule; the feeling is only painful (dukkha).

Sāvatthī · Jetavana monastery

In the cold season, monks spread out lodging furniture in the open air and warmed their bodies. Then they left without putting it away and without asking anyone, so the furniture got wet in the rain. The Blessed One laid down the training rule:

The training rule“Yo pana bhikkhu saṅghikaṃ mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā bhisiṃ vā kocchaṃ vā ajjhokāse santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā taṃ pakkamanto neva uddhareyya na uddharāpeyya, anāpucchaṃ vā gaccheyya, pācittiyaṃ.”

Later he gave this allowance: during the eight months when one is not in the rains retreat, lodging furniture may be kept in a pavilion marked as avassika saṅketa, or at the foot of a tree where crows do not sit.

WordMeaning
SaṅghikaThings that belong to the Saṅgha.
Mañca, pīṭhaAny bed made in the form of a mañca is a mañca; it is the same for a pīṭha.
BhisiA seat made by preparing a cover of cloth or of allowable leather and filling it with wool, leaves, grass, bark, cloth and so on. It is proper for sitting and for lying down; there is no size limit.
KocchaA seat made by wrapping bark, usīra, muñja, pabbaja and so on inside and tying it, shaped like a drum, with lion skin and so on around the middle. In using lodging furniture there is no unallowable skin; even if it is made of gold, it is proper.

Ajjhokāsa — In the four months of the rains, even if no rain falls, it is not proper to spread [furniture] in an ordinary open space or in a pavilion where rain falls. In countries where rain falls in the cold season, it is also not proper in the other four months. In the hot season it is proper. At the foot of a tree where crows and other birds always live, it is never proper. All such places and times where it is not proper to spread are counted as “ajjhokāsa”.

Santharitvā — having spread it, for oneself or for others.

Santharāpetvā — having had it spread by an unordained person (the responsibility, palibodha, is his own); if an ordained monk spread it, the responsibility is on the one who spread it.

Anāpucchaṃ gaccheyya — if, without asking a conscientious monk, a novice, or a monastery helper, without putting it away, he goes without concern and goes beyond a leḍḍupāta (a stone's throw): with the first step, dukkaṭa; with the second step, pācittiya. For one who, from the dining hall, sends word, “Set it up in such-and-such a place,” and goes to another place, the offence should be fixed by the lifting of the feet (pāduddhāra).

secs.t: (B) The laying down of the rule and the command
secs.h:
It was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning many monks.

It is a common rule; it is anāṇattika; it is a tika-pācittiya. For a personal object it is a tika-dukkaṭa.

secs.t: (C) Division of offences — according to the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
secs.h:
CaseOffence
Spreading the Saṅgha's mañca, pīṭha, bhisi or koccha in the open, and going beyond a stone's throw without putting it away and without asking (in all three perceptions about “belonging to the Saṅgha”)Pācittiya
first step dukkaṭa; second step pācittiya
Leaving in the open a cimilikā, uttarattharaṇa, bhūmattharaṇa, taṭṭikā, cammakkhaṇḍa, pādapuñchana, phalakapīṭha, other wooden / clay items, or even a bowl standDukkaṭa
Leaving another person's things in the openDukkaṭa
Leaving one's own personal thingsNo offence

Anāpatti

CaseResult
Going after leaving it in a personal place or a trusted place.No offence
Going with the intention of coming back, after putting the lodging furniture away, or after leaving it in the sun to dry.No offence
A senior monk comes and makes him get up.No offence
Being hindered by non-humans, wild animals, or powerful people.No offence
Sudden dangers to life or to the holy life; and being insane.No offence

1
The mañca and so on belong to the Saṅgha.
2
They have been spread, or had spread, in the open.
3
Not being palibuddha.
4
No danger.
5
Being without concern (nirapekkha).
6
Going beyond a stone's throw (leḍḍupāta).
The same as in the first Kaṭhina rule; it is kiriyā-akiriyā.

Sāvatthī · Jetavana monastery

The group-of-seventeen monks spread out bedding in a dwelling that belonged to the Saṅgha, and left without putting it away and without asking anyone, so it was eaten by termites. The Blessed One laid down the training rule:

The training rule“Yo pana bhikkhu saṅghike vihāre seyyaṃ santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā taṃ pakkamanto neva uddhareyya na uddharāpeyya, anāpucchaṃ vā gaccheyya, pācittiyaṃ.”

“In a dwelling” means in a room, or in a lodging that is fully enclosed and covered. The ten kinds of seyyā:

SeyyāMeaning
BhisiThe seat filled with wool and so on, as said in the previous rule.
CimilikāA spread made to protect the colour of a prepared floor.
UttarattharaṇaA covering (paccattharaṇa) spread on top of beds, chairs and so on.
BhūmattharaṇaMats (kaṭasāraka) and so on, spread on top of the cimilikā when there is one, or on the clean floor when there is not.
TaṭṭikāA taṭṭikā made of palm leaves and so on.
CammakkhaṇḍaAny piece of skin. Only carrying lion skin and the like is forbidden; in using lodging furniture there is no unallowable skin.
NisīdanaWell known.
PaccattharaṇaA pāvāra, a kojava.
TiṇasanthāraWell known.
PaṇṇasanthāraWell known.

Taking one of these from his own share by seniority (vassagga), he spreads it, or has it spread, in a dwelling of the stated kind. If a monk who is leaving for another place goes without keeping it safe from termites, without putting it away, and without asking — then, when he goes beyond the enclosure (parikkhepa) of an enclosed monastery, or the precinct (upacāra) of an unenclosed one: with the first step, dukkaṭa; with the second step, pācittiya. In a place where there is no fear of termites, it is proper to go even without asking; asking is a duty (vatta).

secs.t: (B) The laying down of the rule and the command
secs.h:
It was laid down at Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-seventeen monks.

It is a common rule; it is anāṇattika; it is a tika-pācittiya. For a personal object it is a tika-dukkaṭa.

secs.t: (C) Division of offences — according to the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī
secs.h:
CaseOffence
Spreading bedding in a Saṅgha dwelling and going beyond the monastery's enclosure / precinct without putting it away and without asking (in all three perceptions)Pācittiya
first step dukkaṭa; second step pācittiya
Spreading bedding in the precinct of the dwelling, in the assembly hall, in a pavilion that is not enclosed (or where many people gather), or at the foot of a tree, and going without askingDukkaṭa
Spreading a bed or chair in the dwelling / precinct / assembly hall / pavilion / foot of a tree, and going without askingDukkaṭa
With regard to another person's thingsDukkaṭa
With regard to one's own personal thingsNo offence

Anāpatti

CaseResult
Place and putting away: keeping it in a personal / trusted place, or going after putting it away.No offence
Change of journey: going with the intention of coming back that same day, then the journey changes, and he has someone else put it away.No offence
Obstacles: being unable to come back because of floods, fear of kings / thieves, wild animals, or obstacles from non-humans.No offence
Dangers and insanity: in sudden dangers, and when insane.No offence

1
It is bedding of the stated kind.
2
It belongs to the Saṅgha.
3
It has been spread, or had spread, in a dwelling of the stated kind.
4
Not being palibuddha.
5
No danger.
6
Going away without concern (anapekkha).
7
Going beyond the limit of the precinct.
It should be understood in the same way as said in the previous (anantara) rule.
